items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: I just feel that they’ve learned things almost by rote, by too much Arban book and not enough simple stuff.

ctx.x: Well I guess I look at all the players coming out of the jazz programs and many of them are really, really good. I’m wondering where they’re going to go with it if there’s no audience for it, and if there’s something we could do, and I guess what you’re doing here with the Swing Street —

I don’t, you know I think a lot of the teacher’s don’t really have, are that fully aware of what the world is like out there as a jazz musician, I mean the communication part of it, having to sell your product. Technique is not the only answer. I have to be careful because I don’t want to, I don’t know enough about what is being taught really. I do know it’s kind of simplistic to say that you’re turning out great technicians, but I don’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

think enough time is spent on collective improvisation, small band work. The real world, let’s face it, is not going to be a big band reading those parts. And I do not like a lot of the solos put out by great technicians, I just feel that they’ve learned things almost by rote, by too much Arban book and not enough simple stuff. All the things I’ve been talking about. My whole philosophy I think a lot of it is lacking in the music school. We didn’t have that much in music schools, because we did it by playing. Of…
